The Wolf Also Shall Dwell With the Lamb
thuh WOOLF AWL-soh shal DWEL with thuh LAM
n. phr. (Isaiah's picture of the peace of the Messiah's reign)
Hebrew we-gar ze'eb im keves — gur, to sojourn or dwell as a guest; ze'eb, wolf; keves, a lamb; the verb is the one used of a stranger lodging peaceably in another's land.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

After the rod out of the stem of Jesse and the Spirit resting upon Him, Isaiah describes the peace of His reign: “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.” Each pair sets a predator beside its natural prey, and the verb is the gentle one — the wolf sojourns with the lamb, lodging as a guest where he would have eaten. The passage gives its own ground in the ninth verse: they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. Enmity ends because the knowledge of God fills the earth. Reformed expositors have read the picture in two complementary ways and both are in Scripture. It describes the character of Christ's kingdom already begun, where wolves are not caged but changed — Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle, which is a wolf dwelling with lambs in the only way that lasts. And it looks on to the new heavens and new earth, where Isaiah repeats the words and adds that the wolf and the lamb shall feed together and dust shall be the serpent's meat. The one thing the passage will not support is a peace without the knowledge of the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Wolf, a beast of prey of the canine kind, fierce and ravenous. Lamb, the young of the sheep kind. The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, Isaiah 11:6, the peace of the Messiah's reign where the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD.

Wolf, a beast of prey of the canine kind, fierce, ravenous, and bold.

Lamb, the young of the sheep kind; in Scripture, the figure of meekness.

Hebrew gur, to sojourn or lodge as a guest in another's place.

Hebrew ze'eb, wolf; keves, a lamb; namer, the leopard of the next clause.

Grounded in the earth full of the knowledge of the LORD, Isaiah 11:9.

Key Scripture

Isa 11:6 — "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them."

Isa 11:9 — "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."

Isa 11:1 — "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:"

Isa 65:25 — "The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock: and dust shall be the serpent's meat. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The passage is pressed into a political programme of peace without Christ, and on the other side locked into a single future millennial literalism that silences its present force.

expand to see more

Quoted at interfaith gatherings and on peace posters, the verse is regularly used to commend a reconciliation of parties that has nothing to do with the Messiah whose reign produces it. Isaiah will not be quarried that way. The chapter opens with the rod out of the stem of Jesse on whom the Spirit of the LORD rests, who judges with righteousness and smites the earth with the rod of his mouth; the peace of the sixth verse is the fruit of that Person's government, and the ninth verse names the cause as the knowledge of the LORD covering the earth. A peace sought apart from Him is the prophets' false peace, crying peace, peace, when there is no peace.

The dispensational handling errs by restricting the passage to a future earthly millennium and so removing every present claim it has on the church. Scripture itself applies Isaiah 11 to the time of the gospel: Paul quotes the eleventh chapter's root of Jesse to prove that the Gentiles now hope in Him. The Reformed reading holds both the already and the not yet — the kingdom has come in Christ and wolves are being changed now, and the full picture waits for the new heavens and new earth, where Isaiah says the same thing again. The principle to recover is that the enmity ends by conversion and consummation, not by negotiation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gur, to sojourn as a guest; ze'eb, wolf; keves, lamb — predators lodging with prey, grounded in the earth's fulness of the knowledge of the LORD.

expand to see more

Hebrew gur, to sojourn or lodge as a guest, not merely to coexist.

Hebrew ze'eb, the wolf, a standing figure for the ravenous enemy of the flock.

Hebrew keves, a lamb; with namer, leopard, and gedi, kid, in the same verse.

Hebrew da'ath YHWH, the knowledge of the LORD, named as the cause, Isaiah 11:9.

Repeated of the new heavens and new earth, Isaiah 65:25.
